name: You Publish
tagline: A hosted tool for writing posts and publishing them to your own site without touching a build pipeline.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Publishing text to the internet is the single most solved problem in web development, and an agent can scaffold the whole thing before your coffee cools. A static site generator plus a markdown folder plus an RSS feed covers the actual core loop: write, preview, publish. What a hosted tool sells is the part after that, namely the domain, the TLS cert, the build that runs when you hit a button, and the fact that nothing breaks when you ignore it for six months. If you already own a domain and tolerate a git push, the DIY version is not a compromise, it is the normal way. If the appeal was never writing a config file again, pay the money and keep writing.
coreLoopDIY: Write markdown in a folder, hit publish, get a fast static blog with clean URLs, an RSS feed, and a sitemap.
requirements: A domain name if you want a real URL
Any static host (Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, GitHub Pages) or a VPS
whatYouLose: Hosting, TLS, and CDN handled for you; now that is your job forever
Writing from a phone, unless you enjoy editing markdown in a mobile git client
Any built-in audience, discovery feed, or subscriber list
A WYSIWYG editor with image uploads that just work
Someone else to blame when a deploy fails at 1am
moatNotes: The moat on hosted publishing tools is almost never the editor, it is the operational boredom they absorb: certs, builds, redirects, uptime.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the build is cheap and the maintenance is not. A static blog you generate in an afternoon will work perfectly for two months and then sit there as a small nagging obligation: the Node version drifts, a dependency throws a deprecation, your host changes its default branch behavior, and suddenly publishing a paragraph is a forty minute errand. Paying someone to keep the publish button working is a reasonable trade for people whose actual product is the writing. It is a bad trade for people who already live in a terminal.
notes: The honest test: if you have deployed a static site before, you will never open the hosted version again.
prompt:
Build a personal publishing system as a static site. Stack: Astro 4 with content collections, TypeScript, plain CSS. No React, no Tailwind, no CMS, no database, no accounts.

Structure:
- src/content/posts/*.md with frontmatter: title, description, date, draft (boolean), tags (string array), slug (optional override).
- Zod schema in src/content/config.ts validating that frontmatter. Build must fail loudly on a bad post.
- Pages: / (post list, newest first, drafts excluded in production), /posts/[slug], /tags/[tag], /about.
- /rss.xml via @astrojs/rss and /sitemap.xml via @astrojs/sitemap.
- 404 page.

Writing experience:
- A Node script at scripts/new-post.mjs that takes a title, slugifies it, and writes a dated markdown file with filled frontmatter, then prints the path.
- npm run dev shows drafts. npm run build excludes them.
- Support markdown images from /public/images and code blocks with Shiki syntax highlighting.
- Reading time estimate on each post, computed at build time from word count.

Design: one stylesheet, system font stack, max 70ch measure, dark mode via prefers-color-scheme. Readable, not fancy. No web fonts, no layout shift, no JavaScript shipped to the browser unless a feature genuinely needs it (it does not).

SEO basics: per-page title and description, canonical link, Open Graph and Twitter card tags pulled from frontmatter, a site config file holding siteUrl, author, and title.

Deployment: output static files to dist/. Include a netlify.toml and a GitHub Actions workflow that builds and deploys on push to main. Put siteUrl in .env.example, never hardcode secrets.

Out of scope: comments, analytics, newsletter signup, search, an admin UI, multi-author support.

Finish with a README: how to write a post, how to preview, how to publish, and how to point a domain at it.
